title: The protocol you use all day
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read an HTTP exchange by hand, explain where the time in a request actually goes, and say what changed between the versions you will encounter.

blocks.text: HTTP sits directly on the connection you built in this module. In its original form it is text you could type yourself: a request line, some headers, a blank line, and optionally a body. Everything the web does is built on that, and knowing the shape lets you diagnose problems without a browser in the way.

blocks.caption: Captured from a live server
lines: Transfer-Encoding: chunked      <- length not known up front; sent in pieces
Connection: keep-alive          <- reuse this connection for the next request
Age: 4588                       <- this answer has been cached for 4588 seconds
cf-cache-status: HIT            <- and it was served from that cache

blocks.text: Two of those headers tell a story worth reading. Transfer-Encoding says the server did not know the size in advance and sent the body in pieces — the length-prefix problem from the capstone, solved at the protocol level. Age and the cache status say this response never reached the origin server at all.

rows: Submit; may create or change something

blocks.title: That last column is what the retry lesson needed
blocks.text: Whether an operation can be safely repeated decides whether a client may retry it after a timeout. GET, PUT and DELETE can be repeated with the same end result; POST generally cannot, which is why a failed payment cannot simply be retried by the client and why systems that must retry give each request a unique key the server remembers.

rows: Look elsewhere, or use your cached copy
Your request was wrong — do not retry unchanged
Their problem — retrying with backoff may work

blocks.text: The 4xx and 5xx split is the practical one: a 4xx will fail again identically, while a 5xx may succeed on a later attempt. That maps directly onto the retry rules from the error-handling lesson.

blocks.caption: Measured phases of one https request
lines: dns        2.5 ms   the name lookup from the previous lesson
firstbyte  121 ms   the server thinking and the first bytes arriving
# TLS fell from 308 ms to 50 ms because the session was resumed.

blocks.title: This is the answer to the question from the first lesson
blocks.text: The very first exercise in this course asked why running the same curl twice makes the second faster, and said the answer involved DNS caching, connection setup and TLS. Here it is measured: the name was already cached, and the encryption negotiation was resumed instead of performed from scratch. Notice also that setup dominated — of 473 ms, only about 121 ms was the server producing an answer.
Why connection reuse matters so much

Every new connection costs the handshake plus, for https, the encryption negotiation. A page that fetches thirty resources over thirty connections pays that thirty times. Keep-alive reuses one connection for many requests, and this is the single largest reason a modern page loads faster than the same page would have in 1997.

rows: Many requests in parallel on one connection, compressed headers
The same, over UDP instead of TCP
One lost packet stalling everything else

blocks.text: Verified: the request measured above negotiated HTTP/2. You do not usually choose this — client and server agree during the encryption negotiation, and the version in use is something to check rather than assume.

blocks.title: HTTP/3 is where the UDP lesson pays off
blocks.text: In TCP, one lost packet holds up everything behind it, because the protocol must deliver bytes in order. When several independent requests share one connection, a loss affecting one of them stalls all of them. HTTP/3 moves to UDP and manages ordering per stream instead, so a loss affects only the stream it belongs to. This is the concrete reason the first lesson said UDP is not 'TCP without the good parts'.

blocks.title: Speak HTTP by hand
steps:
Run: printf 'GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Connection: close

' | nc example.com 80
Read the status line, the headers, the blank line and the body — that is the entire protocol
Try it without the Host header and observe the error a server gives
Run: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://example.com    and identify Transfer-Encoding and Connection
Run: curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'dns=%{time_namelookup} connect=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} total=%{time_total}\n' https://example.com
Run it twice more and watch the TLS phase fall
Run: curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'version=%{http_version}\n' https://example.com    and note which version was agreed
Run: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com/nothing-here    and classify the code
blocks.expected: An HTTP exchange you typed yourself, a timing breakdown showing setup dominating the total, and a TLS phase that shrinks on the second request. Having spoken the protocol by hand once is what makes reading a capture or a server log straightforward afterwards.

cheatsheet: HTTP is text on top of the connection: request line, headers, blank line, body
Transfer-Encoding: chunked means the length was not known in advance
Connection: keep-alive means the connection is reused for the next request
GET, PUT, DELETE and HEAD are safe to repeat; POST generally is not
4xx will fail again identically; 5xx may succeed on retry with backoff
Measured: dns 2.5 ms, connect 41 ms, TLS 308 ms, server 121 ms — setup dominated
On the second request TLS fell to about 50 ms because the session was resumed
HTTP/1.1 added keep-alive; HTTP/2 multiplexes; HTTP/3 moves to UDP
HTTP/3 exists because one lost TCP packet stalls every request sharing the connection

checkpoint.prompt: A request takes 473 ms in total, of which 121 ms is the server producing an answer. Where did the rest go?
checkpoint.explanation: Measured: dns 2.5 ms, connect 41 ms, TLS 308 ms. Setup dominated, which is exactly why connection reuse and session resumption make such a visible difference. That is: the name lookup, the connection handshake, and negotiating encryption.

checkpoint.prompt: A request fails with a timeout. Which methods can a client safely retry?
checkpoint.explanation: This is the retry rule from the error-handling lesson applied to HTTP. When a POST must be retried, the usual answer is a unique key per request that the server remembers. Repeating them produces the same end result, which is why they are safe to retry; POST generally cannot be repeated safely.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does the TLS phase shrink on a second request to the same server?

choices.B: The connection is faster the second time

checkpoint.explanation: Measured: about 308 ms on the first request and about 50 ms on the second. This is one of the three effects the first lesson of this course pointed at without naming. Resumed rather than negotiated again from scratch.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does HTTP/3 use UDP when HTTP has always relied on TCP's reliability?

choices.A: So that the cost of connection setup is avoided entirely
choices.C: UDP is faster in every case
choices.D: A lost packet stalls every request on a TCP connection

checkpoint.explanation: Over UDP, ordering is managed per stream so a loss affects only its own. It rebuilds the reliability it needs on top of UDP, per stream. This is the concrete case behind the first lesson's point that UDP is the right choice when the application can manage recovery better than a general-purpose algorithm.
